forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Essex's 2027/28 budget gap rises to £169m from £108m forecast seven months earlier
news_drafts.lead:
Essex County Council's budget gap for 2027/28 has risen to £169m, 10% of its net budget requirement, from the £108m set out in its 2026/27 Annual Plan seven months earlier. The figure is in the Budget and Medium Term Resource Strategy Update before Cabinet on 6 November.

The paper attributes the increase mainly to demand and inflation across social care. That includes revised inflation assumptions for Adult Social Care and a £29m pressure on Children's placements. The gap is set against a Government funding outlook of no growth across 2026/27 to 2028/29.

The paper models council tax rises of 2%, 3.5% and 5% a year. It states that each 1% uplift missed widens the gap by around £9m a year, and that the Government expects maximum annual increases. At 5% a year, the council says "we would still have budget gaps of £121m in 2027/28 increasing to £266m by 2030/31".
news_drafts.paper_title: Budget and Medium Term Resource Strategy Update (FP/172/09/26)

news_drafts.headline: Essex police absorbs pay costs through accounting change while fire faces £0.5m shortfall
news_drafts.lead: Essex Police and Fire Service have revised their 2027/28 budgets after six months of experience with actual pay costs and demand. Police moved from a projected £1.4m shortfall to a £0.7m surplus between June and September, but £2.8m of that £2.1m improvement came from a change in how the force calculates minimum revenue provision (MRP), the amount set aside each year to pay off past borrowing. The underlying position shifted because staff pay awards reached 3.5 per cent against a 2.5 per cent assumption, costing £2.0m more than forecast, while new service demands added £3.4m pressure. Fire Service moved from a balanced 2027/28 budget in February to a £0.5m shortfall by September after a 3.8 per cent pay award for operational staff cost £0.7m against a 2.2 per cent forecast. Together, the two services faced £2.7m in unfunded pay costs. Police also identified £3.4m in new demand that cannot be contained within existing budgets, a pressure that will persist through the medium-term outlook.

news_drafts.headline: Essex pension fund achieved 108% funding level in 2025 valuation as risks rise
news_drafts.lead: The Essex Pension Fund finished the 2025 triennial valuation overfunded at 108%, meaning pension liabilities are covered with a surplus. The fund has maintained clean internal audit opinions for eight consecutive years, with both its funding and investments functions and its administration receiving Good Assurance ratings in 2025/26 and no audit recommendations issued. However, the fund faces emerging pressures: a February 2026 funding-at-risk measure stood at 26.3%, slightly above the 25% target, indicating solvency is marginally more exposed than the fund's tolerance threshold allows. As of August, 17 strategic risks remained above their target scores, with the fund conducting a full review of its risk register to align with revised strategic objectives and incorporate emerging risks including local government reorganisation and artificial intelligence.

findings.paper_title: Recommissioning of Additional Reablement Capacity (ARC) and contract extension to Home to Assess (H2A) services (FP/166/09/26)
findings.headline: Essex flags a risk that Better Care Fund income for intermediate care could reduce, or that conditions could change, in future years
findings.detail: The paper says the BCF framework and local government settlement preserve planned NHS minimum contribution increases until 2028/29, and continuity of funding is assumed in the MTRS. Any shortfall in later years would need to be managed by partners within the pooled budget.
findings.matters: Pooled-budget income that is only protected to 2028/29 is a funding horizon a council's finance director, and any lender assessing the council's medium-term position, would want to know.
findings.figures: NHS minimum contribution increases preserved until 2028/29
findings.quote: There is a risk that the funding available through the BCF will reduce, or that conditions will change in future years as part of wider reforms.

findings.paper_title: Recommissioning of Additional Reablement Capacity (ARC) and contract extension to Home to Assess (H2A) services (FP/166/09/26)
findings.headline: Government withdrew the previous Essex local government reorganisation decision on 7 September 2026, pending a review
findings.detail: The paper says the Government announced that the previous LGR decision for Essex had been withdrawn and that shadow council elections will not take place in 2027. The timing and scope of the review are awaited. The paper says the ARC lot structure has been designed to transfer to any successor organisations.
findings.matters: A change to the expected structure of local government in Essex affects who holds the contracts and the funding commitments a lender or finance director is assessing.
findings.quote: The Government announced on 7 September 2026 that the previous decision on LGR within Essex had been withdrawn, pending a review

findings.paper_title: Recommissioning of Additional Reablement Capacity (ARC) and contract extension to Home to Assess (H2A) services (FP/166/09/26)
findings.headline: Essex reports ARC activity has fluctuated more than originally anticipated, with demand below contracted levels at times and above capacity at others
findings.detail: The paper links these fluctuations to the decision to reduce block hours and raise tolerance. It says the change is meant to reduce the risk of paying for unused block capacity and reduce reliance on spot-purchased domiciliary care when providers cannot meet demand.
findings.matters: Block contracts that do not match demand create either paid-for voids or costly spot purchasing, and the paper shows a council adjusting its contract design in response.
findings.quote: Current ARC contracts have experienced greater fluctuations in activity than originally anticipated

findings.paper_title: Recommissioning of Additional Reablement Capacity (ARC) and contract extension to Home to Assess (H2A) services (FP/166/09/26)
findings.headline: Expected cost of the new ARC contracts is £6.7m a year before savings, with the paper noting price risk above current assumptions
findings.detail: The paper estimates annual cost at current average weekly hours, assuming current hourly rates plus inflation to 2027/28. Actual rates will depend on the tender outcome. The paper says tendered prices above these assumptions would raise ARC costs and the savings needed. Price carries 70% of the evaluation weighting.
findings.matters: A tender result above the modelled rate would widen the savings gap, so the price assumption is one a finance director would test against other councils' reablement tenders.
findings.figures: £6.7m expected annual cost of new ARC service before savings and change activity; ARC price weighting 70%
findings.quote: the expected cost of the recommendation to tender a new ARC service is £6.7m per year before savings and change activity.

findings.paper_title: Recommissioning of Additional Reablement Capacity (ARC) and contract extension to Home to Assess (H2A) services (FP/166/09/26)
findings.headline: Maximum decision value of £28.9m across new ARC contracts (£22.1m) and H2A extensions (£6.8m) to 2030/31
findings.detail: The paper gives the maximum value of the recommendations by year. New ARC contracts account for £22.1m, with a peak of £7.4m in each of 2028/29 and 2029/30. H2A extensions account for £6.8m over 2028/29 and 2029/30. The contract values exclude inflationary uplifts.
findings.matters: The maximum commitment in the decision sets the upper bound on new contract spend, which other councils running similar reablement procurements can compare against.
findings.figures: £28.9m total maximum decision value; ARC (new contracts) £22.1m; H2A (extensions) £6.8m; annual totals £4.1m (2027/28), £10.8m (2028/29), £10.8m (2029/30), £3.3m (2030/31)
